subject: geography
title: Fieldwork Adventure: Data Presentation
welcome_lead: Numbers tell stories — but only if you pick the right graph. Time to choose wisely.
meta_desc: GCSE Geography data presentation — scatter, bar, line, pie, choropleth, isoline maps.
final_note: You learned the main graph and map types and when to use each.

concepts.def: Shows change over time — continuous data
Shows proportions of a whole — percentages
Bar chart drawn on a map at sample location

walkthroughs.body_html:
Bar chart: comparing categories (e.g. pedestrians in 5 streets).

Line graph: change over time (river discharge through the day).

Scatter graph: relationship (river depth vs distance downstream).

Pie chart: parts of a whole (% by land use).

Choropleth: shaded map — e.g. average house price by ward. Darker = higher. Easy to read, hides within-area variation.

Isoline map: lines join equal values (like contour lines or pressure isobars).

Dot map: a dot for each unit (e.g. 1 dot = 100 people).

Located bar/pie: place chart at each sample site on a base map.

When describing a graph, use the acronym TEA:

Trend (overall pattern).
Evidence (use figures).
Anomalies (outliers).

For a scatter: state direction (positive/negative), strength (strong/weak), and quote any outliers with their value.

mcqs.q: Which graph BEST shows the RELATIONSHIP between two variables?
What does a CHOROPLETH map use to show data?

numericals.q: On a pie chart showing 25% urban, 30% rural, 45% suburban — how many DEGREES is the suburban slice (round to nearest)?

free_texts.q: What type of map joins points of EQUAL VALUE with lines (e.g. contour, isobar)? One word starting with 'i'.
